Affiliation: Miguel Altamirano Cabrera and Dzmitry Tsetserukou Abstract Simulation enables scalable training of Vision-Language-Action policies by using privileged experts to generate visual demonstrations without requiring every trajectory to be collected through manual teleoperation. However, such pipelines typically retain successful demonstrations while failed rollouts are discarded, even though they expose precisely the off-nominal states from which recovery must be learned. We introduce Kintsugi-VLA, a framework for converting failed rollouts into targeted synthetic recovery data by exploiting exact state restoration and branching in simulation. For a fixed privileged expert, we define interventional recoverability as the probability of completing the original task after the simulator is restored to a given state, estimate it using adaptive Monte Carlo continuations with pointwise Wilson intervals, and characterize its non-monotonic evolution along failed trajectories. These estimates identify an observed terminal low-recoverability frontier—the point after which measured recoverability remains below a threshold—which is then used to select informative recovery starting states. In a simulated Franka manipulation task, targeted recovery data yield aggregate SmolVLA recovery success of 34.6% and 38.4% under difficulty- and frame-budget matching, respectively, 5.8 and 6.7 percentage points above uniform sampling within the same recovery window. The same ordering is observed under disturbed end-to-end execution and shifted clutter and physics conditions, while clean-task success decreases from 76.8% to 74.7%. Kintsugi-VLA demonstrates how failed simulator rollouts can be transformed from discarded experience into structured recovery-training data through direct interventional measurement. I INTRODUCTION Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map multimodal observations and language instructions to robot actions and have become a promising approach to general-purpose manipulation [ 1 , 2 ] . Simulation and automated data-generation pipelines can reduce the amount of manual robot data collection by using privileged controllers to generate visual demonstrations at scale [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . In our setting, a privileged simulation expert generates both nominal and recovery demonstrations through the same virtual camera interface used to train the VLA, without human teleoperation. Success-only demonstration collection, however, leaves failed rollouts unused for imitation even though they contain states that are poorly represented by nominal trajectories. Missed grasps, unintended object motion, collisions, or stalled progress can move the policy away from its training distribution. Rather than imitating the failed actions themselves, we use these rollouts as sources of states from which new successful recovery demonstrations can be generated. Existing work addresses failure through detection, recovery-data collection, or inference-time correction [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . We focus on an upstream question: given a failed simulator rollout, from which states should recovery demonstrations be collected? The final failed state may already be difficult to recover from, whereas states selected too early may largely repeat nominal behavior. Simulation provides a direct way to examine this trade-off: a saved state can be restored and the same privileged expert can be executed from it repeatedly. Fig. 1: Failed rollouts as recovery-data sources. Kintsugi-VLA restores saved simulator states and repeatedly tests expert continuations to identify states suitable for synthetic recovery demonstrations. Kintsugi-VLA uses this capability to measure expert-relative recoverability along failed trajectories. For each candidate checkpoint, we restore the simulator state and repeatedly transfer control to a fixed recovery expert. The fraction of successful continuations estimates p rec E p_{\mathrm{rec}}^{E} , the probability that the specified expert completes the original task under the specified restoration and continuation protocol. These measurements characterize recovery structure and define candidate regions from which complete successful expert continuations are recorded as synthetic recovery demonstrations for VLA adaptation. Our contributions are: • a restore-and-branch procedure that turns failed simulator rollouts into recovery-training data; • an analysis of expert-relative recoverability, including uncertainty, non-monotonicity, recovery islands, and expert dependence; • closed-loop SmolVLA evaluation under matched recovery-difficulty and visual-data budgets, where targeted selection achieves 34.6% and 38.4% recovery success versus 28.8% and 31.7% for uniform selection. II RELATED WORK Synthetic and corrective data generation. Simulation and automated data-generation methods can scale robot-learning datasets while reducing manual demonstration effort [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . IntervenGen generates corrective intervention data to improve imitation-policy robustness [ 12 ] , while RaC fine-tunes policies using recovery-and-correction trajectories collected around failed execution [ 13 ] . Kintsugi-VLA addresses the same broader problem of exploiting non-nominal experience, but uses simulator restoration to repeatedly test failed-rollout states under a privileged expert and uses the measured recoverability to select states for synthetic recovery-data collection. Failure detection and recovery. SAFE predicts VLA failure likelihood from internal representations [ 6 ] , while RACER augments imitation learning with language-guided recovery trajectories [ 7 ] . B2FF selects familiar visual milestones for inference-time recovery [ 8 ] , CoRe uses counterfactual continuation and realignment [ 9 ] , and FLARE combines failure monitoring with retry and reset behaviors [ 10 ] . LIBERO-RECOVER constructs recovery scenarios from failed executions and uses visual-language reasoning for failure localization and characterization [ 11 ] . In contrast, Kintsugi-VLA focuses on an upstream data-generation question: which states from a failed simulator rollout should be used to generate recovery demonstrations for subsequent VLA adaptation. ## Kintsugi-VLA: Turning Failed Robot Rollouts into Recovery Data

The field of robotics is constantly striving for progress, pushing the boundaries of what machines can achieve. However, the journey from a robot's initial design to a fully-fledged, reliable system is rarely straightforward.  Failures are inevitable, and the discarded data from failed rollouts can be a valuable resource for learning.  A new framework, Kintsugi-VLA, is changing the way we approach this challenge.

Kintsugi-VLA, developed by researchers at the Intelligent Space Robotics Laboratory at Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology, tackles the problem of failed robot rollouts.  The system leverages the power of simulation to transform these discarded experiences into structured recovery-training data.  This process, known as interventional recoverability, allows robots to learn from their mistakes and improve their performance in the real world.

The framework works by utilizing a privileged simulation expert. This expert generates both nominal and recovery demonstrations through the same virtual camera interface used to train the VLA.  This allows for the creation of a more realistic and nuanced training environment.  The system then estimates the probability of completing the original task after the simulator is restored to a given state, using adaptive Monte Carlo continuations with pointwise Wilson intervals.  This non-monotonic evolution of recoverability is then used to select informative recovery starting states.

The results are promising.  In a simulated Franka manipulation task, targeted recovery data yielded an aggregate SmolVLA recovery success of 34.6% and 38.4% under difficulty- and frame-budget matching, respectively.  These results are 5.8 and 6.7 percentage points above uniform sampling within the same recovery window.  The same ordering is observed under disturbed end-to-end execution and shifted clutter and physics conditions, while clean-task success decreases from 76.8% to 74.7%.  This demonstrates the effectiveness of Kintsugi-VLA in transforming discarded experience into structured recovery-training data.

Kintsugi-VLA's impact extends beyond the lab.  It offers a new paradigm for robot learning, one that moves beyond the limitations of traditional methods.  By leveraging simulation to transform failed rollouts into valuable recovery data, Kintsugi-VLA paves the way for more robust and reliable robots in the future.  This breakthrough could significantly impact various industries, from manufacturing and logistics to healthcare and agriculture.
